content: There has been a significant increase in the number of newly registered HIV-positive males who have sex with males and transgender individuals at public HIV treatment centers. The National Mental Health Association (NMHA) has been actively working to establish strong linkages and partnerships with organizations such as the National AIDS Control Programme, Rahnuma-Family Planning Association, the Asia-Pacific Coalition on Male Sexual Health, the Asia-Pacific Transgender Network, and Youth Voices Count, among other stakeholders. A multi-partner project led by the South African National AIDS Council (SANAC) and the Department of Health (DoH) has developed an integrated approach to educate healthcare providers on issues affecting key populations. This initiative also aims to empower public health staff to interact appropriately, both in terms of attitude and clinical expertise, with individuals from these communities. Training sessions have been conducted to prepare for the implementation of the National Operational Guidelines for HIV, STI, and TB Programmes for Key Populations in South Africa. The program includes in-person training and mentoring. Thirty trainers participated in an initial training of trainers workshop and were connected to local training centers and health facilities. These trainers subsequently trained 420 healthcare workers over six months. In areas where these training sessions were conducted, members of key populations reported improvements in healthcare workers’ attitudes. Community trust in healthcare providers has increased, as has the utilization of health facilities where sensitization training was linked with peer outreach and HIV prevention education activities conducted by civil society organizations. Further evaluation is planned to guide the scale-up of these efforts. Kimara Peers, a community-based NGO in a low-income area of Dar es Salaam, implements HIV prevention programs. They have established two drop-in centers (DICs) near state-run health centers and dispensaries to provide outreach and services to people who use drugs, particularly those who inject drugs, including individuals aged 16–24 years. The DICs also serve young people engaged in sex work, as there is an overlap between these populations. The staff at the DICs includes trained community outreach workers from the local area and a professional social worker. Outreach workers promote DIC services within the community and during larger public gatherings, such as World Drug Day. Services offered at the DICs include individual and group psychosocial therapy and support, basic information on harm reduction, HIV and STI prevention, condom use, and prevention of viral hepatitis. Referrals are made for methadone-assisted therapy and STI treatment. Educational materials tailored for young people on sexual and reproductive health, including HIV, are available. Referrals to government hospitals are made only with the young person’s consent, and confidentiality is maintained unless the individual permits their parents or family members to be informed or involved. The program is seeking government approval to provide clean needles and syringes at the DICs and through outreach workers. Save the Children uses information and communication technologies (ICT) to enhance HIV prevention outreach to young men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender individuals in Chiang Mai, Thailand. This city is a major destination for sex tourism and has a significant population of migrants from minority ethnic groups and Myanmar. The project disseminates information on HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support through social media platforms commonly used by the MSM community, such as Facebook, Line (a mobile app), and other websites and forums. Research conducted by the project indicated that non-HIV-related content, such as personal grooming, religious instruction, and topical news, could effectively engage young MSM and transgender individuals. Content is developed by project staff based on discussions with volunteers and community members and is regularly updated to remain relevant and engaging. Outreach workers promote Mplus Chat, an app developed by a local NGO working with MSM groups. Educators use this app to establish relationships with young MSM and transgender individuals. Outreach workers are equipped with tablet computers, which help capture the attention of young community members and facilitate communication in noisy environments like bars and clubs. The tablets are used to showcase the project’s website, provide discussion content, and record contact details for follow-up. After initial contact, outreach workers continue to use ICT platforms to disseminate information on HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support. Young MSM and transgender individuals value ongoing online contact as a way to build trust with a counselor while maintaining a degree of anonymity. This relationship enables outreach workers to promote accompanied referrals to free HIV testing. The Test, Connect & Treat program of the New York State Department of Health targets high-risk adolescents and young adults aged 13–24 years for HIV testing. Young males who have sex with males represent the majority of new HIV diagnoses in the state. The program emphasizes a wide range of low-threshold services. Those who test positive for HIV are immediately linked to care, while those who test negative are provided with risk reduction and prevention information and referrals to community services. The program operates through 14 Specialized Care Centers across the state, where multidisciplinary staff teams provide comprehensive and coordinated HIV and primary healthcare, mental health, and supportive services on-site. Clinic services are made accessible through evening and weekend hours and walk-in appointments. Services are provided regardless of the young person’s ability to pay, and those without health insurance are assisted in applying for benefits and enrolling in a managed care plan. For those eligible through their parents, providers ensure confidentiality. If a young person tests positive for HIV, they are given a medical appointment and connected to a social worker and a medical case manager. The program has established partnerships with youth-friendly clinical care and social service providers. Case management assessments focus on the young person’s strengths and self-management skills, including their ability to attend medical appointments and adhere to treatment, which may be hindered by significant mental health, trauma, and substance abuse issues. Case management has been found to be critical for adherence to treatment plans and positive health outcomes. Globally, hundreds of programs are addressing the needs of key population communities who often live outside the reach of formal health and social welfare systems. These programs aim to ensure access to essential HIV and STI prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care that have been available to the general public for decades in many places. Faced with various social, legal, and logistical constraints, these programs are developing innovative ways to reach and encourage service uptake by individuals who may be reluctant to expose themselves to harassment, discrimination, and legal consequences often associated with accessing health and social services. The interventions highlighted in this compilation represent the forefront of a new approach to HIV response, recognizing the importance of critical enablers, innovation, and courage in delivering services for key populations. While the case studies presented are limited in scope and detail, readers are encouraged to contact these programs for more information and inspiration to advance this work.
